title: Creation is not to be worshipped
source_text: Εἴρηται δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω περὶ Περσῶν πρὸς τὸ νεὼς μὲν αὐτοὺς μὴ ἱδρύεσθαι σέβειν δὲ τὸν ἥλιον καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δημιουργήματα· ὅπερ ἡμῖν ἀπαγορεύεται. διδασκομένοις μὴ λατρεύειν „τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα“ ἀλλ᾿ εἰδέναι μὲν ὅτι „ἡ κτίσις ἐλευθερωθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῆς δόξης τῶν τέκνων τοῦ θεοῦ“ καὶ ὅτι „ἡ ἀποκαραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπεκδέχεται“ καὶ ὅτι „τῇ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη, οὐχ ἑκοῦσα ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι.“ καὶ μὴ μὴν καὶ δεῖν τὰ ἐπὶ· τῇ δουλείᾳ „τῆς φθορᾶς“ καὶ ἐπὶ „τῇ ματαιότητι“ ὑποτεταγμένα καὶ „ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι“ κρείττονι ταῦτα πράττοντα ἐν χώρᾳ τιμᾶν θεοῦ τοῦ ἀνενδεοῦς ἢ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ καὶ πρωτοτόκου „πάσης κτίσεως.“ ἀρκεῖ τοίνυν πρὸς ἐκείνοις καὶ ταῦτα περὶ τοῦ Περσῶν ἔθνους. βωμοὺς καὶ ἀγάλματα ἐκτρεπομένων λατρευόντων δὲ „τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα.“ ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τὴν Ἡρακλείτου παρέθετο λέξιν, ὑποδιηγησάμενος αὐτὴν ὑποσημαίνουσαν ἠλίθιον εἶναι τὸ „τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν“ εὔχεσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ γινώσκῃ τις „θεοὺς καὶ ἥρωας, οἵτινές εἰσι,“ λεκτέον ὅτι γινώσκειν μὲν ἔστι θεὸν καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ αὐτοῦ καὶ τοὺς τετιμημένους ὑπὸ θεοῦ τῇ θεὸς προσηγορίᾳ καὶ μετέχοντας τῆς θεότητος αὐτοῦ, ἑτέρους ὄντας παρὰ πάντας τοὺς θεοὺς „τῶν ἐθνῶν,“ „οἵτινές εἰσι“ „δαιμόνια“· οὐ μὴν δυνατόν ἐστι καὶ γινώσκειν τὸν θεὸν καὶ „τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν“ εὔχεσθαι.
pass_a_gloss: It has been said in the things above (ἀνωτέρω) about Persians, regarding their not setting up (ἱδρύω) temples (νεώς) but revering (σέβω) the sun (ἥλιος) and the works of God's making (δημιουργήματα); which is forbidden (ἀπαγορεύω) to us, being taught not to serve (λατρεύω) 'the creature (κτίσις) beside/rather than (παρά) the one who created (κτίσας)', but to know that 'the creation will be freed (ἐλευθερόω) from the bondage (δουλεία) of corruption (φθορά) into the freedom (ἐλευθερία) of the glory (δόξα) of the children (τέκνα) of God' and that 'the eager expectation (ἀποκαραδοκία) of the creation awaits (ἀπεκδέχομαι) the revelation (ἀποκάλυψις) of the sons of God' and that 'to futility (ματαιότης) the creation was subjected (ὑποτάσσω), not willingly (ἑκοῦσα) but because of the one who subjected it, in hope (ἐλπίς)'. And indeed also [that] it is not necessary (δεῖ) to honour (τιμάω) the things subjected to the bondage 'of corruption' and to 'futility' and doing these things 'in hope' of better, in the place (ἐν χώρᾳ) of God the one lacking nothing (ἀνενδεής) or of his Son and firstborn (πρωτότοκος) 'of all creation'. These things then suffice (ἀρκέω), in addition to those, about the nation of the Persians, turning away from altars and images but serving 'the creature rather than the Creator'. And since he also set beside [his argument] (παρατίθημι) the saying (λέξις) of Heraclitus, explaining (ὑποδιηγέομαι) it as hinting (ὑποσημαίνω) that it is foolish (ἠλίθιος) to pray (εὔχομαι) 'to the images' unless one knows 'gods and heroes (ἥρωες), who they are', it must be said that it is possible to know God and his Only-begotten (μονογενής) and those honoured (τιμάω) by God with the appellation (προσηγορία) 'god' and sharing (μετέχω) in his divinity (θεότης), being other than all the gods 'of the nations (ἔθνη)', 'who they are': 'demons (δαιμόνια)'; but it is not possible both to know God and to pray 'to the images'.
pass_b_english: We have spoken earlier about the Persians, on the point that they do not build temples, yet worship the sun and the works that God has made. This is forbidden to us. We are taught not to serve “the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25), but to know that “the creation will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21), and that “the eager expectation of the creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19), and that “the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope” (Romans 8:20). We are taught, moreover, that the things subjected to the bondage “of corruption” (Romans 8:21) and to “futility” (Romans 8:20), which do their work in a better “hope”, must not be honoured in the place of God, who needs nothing, or of his Son, the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). Let this suffice, then, in addition to what was said there, about the Persian nation, who turn away from altars and images but serve “the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25).

Since he also cited the saying of Heraclitus, and explained it as hinting that it is foolish to pray “to images” unless one knows “gods and heroes, who they are” (Heraclitus, fragment B5), we must say this. It is possible to know God, and his Only-begotten, and those whom God has honoured with the title “god” and who share in his divinity. These are different from all “the gods of the nations”; and as for “who they are”, they are “demons” (Psalm 96:5). But it is not possible both to know God and to pray “to images”.

choices.choice: ‘Spoken earlier’: Origen’s earlier remarks on Persian sun-worship (in the books above); no locus added. The transmitted καὶ μὴ μὴν καὶ δεῖν is corrupt; read as καὶ μὴν καὶ μὴ δεῖν, ‘and moreover that ... must not’, which the sense requires. ταῦτα πράττοντα (‘doing these things’) is taken of the heavenly bodies performing their appointed courses ‘in hope’; rendered ‘which do their work’. ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι κρείττονι: κρείττονι agrees with ἐλπίδι, so ‘in a better hope’, not ‘in hope of something better’. The Heraclitus words come through Celsus (7.62), who quoted Heraclitus fragment 22 B5 Diels-Kranz (‘they pray to these images, as if one were to chat with houses, not knowing gods or heroes, who they are’) and said Heraclitus hints that praying to images is foolish; Origen repeats Celsus’s paraphrase. Origen then splices Heraclitus’s ‘who they are’ (οἵτινές εἰσι) with Psalm 95:5 LXX, ‘all the gods of the nations are demons’ (δαιμόνια), English numbering Psalm 96:5 (Hebrew text: ‘idols’). ‘Those whom God has honoured with the title god’: possible uncited allusion to Psalm 82:1, 6 (LXX 81:1, 6, ‘I said, you are gods’); not marked inline because Origen quotes no words. Lowercase ‘god’ there because the title is given to creatures who share God’s divinity, not to God himself.
'in hope of something better' -> 'in a better "hope"' (κρείττονι agrees with ἐλπίδι); note added
Romans 1:25, 8:19-21, Colossians 1:15, Psalm 96:5 (LXX 95:5) and Heraclitus B5 confirmed
